Compiled by the Monk Zhixu of Ancient Wu, explaining the ritual procedures of the *Sūtra on the Divination of the Retribution of Good and Evil Karma*.
First, regarding Dependent Origination:

All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas take pity upon the deluded masses, no less than a mother yearning for her child. Thus, through various skillful means, they teach them how to escape the wheel of suffering.
Yet sentient beings do not understand the causes and conditions of karmic retribution, remaining ignorant of how to sever evil and cultivate goodness.

Excellent. The sun of pure faith has grown dim, and the five turbidities have increased in intensity. Due to the karmic resonance of these extreme sufferings, the response of unconditional compassion becomes doubly urgent.
Thereupon, one suited to this occasion appeared, named Jianjingxin (Firm Pure Faith), who petitioned the World-Honored One for His compassionate salvation.
The Buddha then extensively extolled the merits of Kṣitigarbha and instructed him to establish skillful means; thus, by means of three wheels—
This [text] distinguishes between good and evil through its characteristics. By means of two types of contemplative paths, it leads one back to the single reality realm.
Furthermore, it warns those whose karma is heavy that they must not first cultivate meditative concentration and wisdom; rather, they should rely on the methods of repentance.

Once purity has been attained, they may then practice the two contemplations, which will surely yield results without difficulty. This is truly a divine panacea for the ailments of the degenerate age, and its prescription is as follows:

This is a particularly sublime expedient among all methods. Alas, my own hindrances are deep; I have encountered this period of dharma-disorder. Within the Vinaya teachings and the Chan school, errors and confusions are manifold.
Fortunately, I have met with this scripture, which dispels the clouds of my delusion. Its principles for contemplation and its ritual protocols are now clearly manifest and ready to be practiced.
I humbly observe that while the practice methods across the ten categories of various repentance rites differ slightly in their detail and brevity, each has been set forth here in exhaustive detail.
Doubts have been resolved; I dare not follow my own whims. I therefore describe the *nidāna* (origins) to encourage practice in the second section:
If a disciple of the Buddha wishes to cultivate the supramundane True Dharma, and wishes to be free from all obstructing conditions in the present life—
Those who wish to eliminate the five heinous crimes, the ten evil deeds, and the grave karma of the *ānantarya* offenses;
those who wish to obtain an abundance of all necessities for life; those who wish to cause heavy obstacles and minor hindrances to be entirely extinguished;
those who wish to attain the pure discipline of an *upāsaka*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *bhikṣu*; and those who wish to attain the Bodhisattva’s threefold pure precepts.
Those who wish to attain the various dhyānas and samādhis; those who wish to attain signless wisdom;
those who seek to realize the fruits of the Three Vehicles in this very life; those who wish to be reborn at will in the pure Buddha-lands;

and those who wish to awaken to the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and fully enter the realm of the single reality—all such persons should receive, uphold, and practice this repentance.
This is the Dharma. Why is this? It is because this is the transcendent, expansive compassion of Śākyamuni Tathāgata and the responsive, compassionate vows of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.
There is no suffering from which he does not extract one, and no happiness that he does not bestow. By practicing in accordance with this, one’s pure faith becomes firm and steadfast.
As explained extensively in the sutras, one should believe this with earnest discernment.

Regarding the selection of companions, the third sutra does not specify the number of people; according to the ritual procedures for others, it may reach ten persons, provided they are strictly qualified.
In making your selection, you must seek out those who are vessels of the Dharma. If there are no like-minded companions, it is even better to practice alone.

Should there be those who truly seek liberation from birth and death, they may serve as companions; whether there are ten or fewer people is of no consequence. Furthermore, you must first examine what you seek:
whether it be the Vinaya precepts, meditative concentration and wisdom, the realization of the fruits of the path, or rebirth in a pure land. What you seek...
Only when you are in harmony may you practice together. Among the ten persons, you must further select one of long-standing virtue to serve as the *ācārya* (preceptor).
Regarding ritual conduct and philosophical contemplation, receive these instructions with meticulous care; do not be reckless or negligent, lest your arduous practices be rendered in vain.

Although the fourth method of repentance concerning the marks of the divination wheel is universally intended for sentient beings to disclose their manifold transgressions, each person’s karmic habits from beginningless time have their own particular strengths.
For this reason, the Sūtra first explains the marks of the initial wheel, and only thereafter clarifies [the subsequent methods].

The Method of Repentance: Now, those who wish to practice repentance, having already purified the ritual site (maṇḍala), should, prior to its formal commencement, each occupy a wheel-diagram to discern and examine their good and evil.
One should identify which offenses are particularly grave and repent of them specifically;
this will facilitate the formal confession during the time of practicing repentance. (The method for occupying the diagrams is appended separately below.)
The Fifth Section: The Method for Correctly Practicing Repentance, listed here according to the sutra and consisting of ten categories.
(First: Adorning and Purifying the Ritual Site)

(The Sūtra says: "Those who wish to practice repentance should dwell in a quiet place. According to their means, they should adorn a single room, placing Buddhist ritual objects and installing the scriptures and Dharma within. They should hang silk banners and canopies, and seek out and gather incense and flowers to perform offerings.")

(Second: Purifying the Three Karmas) The Sūtra states: "Bathe the body and wash clothes so as not to allow them to become foul or impure. According to the various rules of practice, whenever one reaches a defiled place, one must change one's garments. Having completed the circumambulation, bathe until pure and put on clean clothes again.

Even if one does not encounter any defilement for an entire day, one must still bathe once. This continues for the duration of the retreat—whether seven days, two weeks, three weeks, or even up to a thousand days—until the signs of the pure wheel of the three karmas are attained. During this time, remain single-mindedly focused."

Regarding idle chatter and all forms of social greetings or inquiries: if there is a need for anything, one may simply request it directly; one must not allow the matter at hand to trigger extraneous conversation. One should maintain single-minded concentration, mindful of the dharma being practiced, and must not for even a moment think of worldly distractions.

One should contemplate the great matter of birth and death and the swift nature of impermanence; only through firm diligence and effort can one achieve success. Should one slightly violate the pure dharma, then all one's labors will be in vain; therefore, one must be careful.
(Third: Offering of Incense and Flowers) (The practitioner first enters the ritual arena.

Proceeding before the Dharma seat, they arrange their seating and straighten their body. With palms joined, they stand leaning slightly. They should first bring to mind all Three Jewels, whose essence is eternally pervasive and omnipresent.

Sentient beings are deluded and wander in saṃsāra—how pitiable! For the sake of these beings, I shall overturn their delusion and lead them back to awakening. Having made this reflection, they should proclaim:)

With all reverence and single-minded devotion, pay homage to the eternally abiding Triple Gem of the ten directions. (Having thus paid homage, one should offer whatever incense, flowers, and so forth are available, making this proclamation:)
Respectfully holding incense and flowers, make offerings according to the Dharma.
May these clouds of incense and flowers pervade the worlds of the ten directions, making offerings to all Buddhas, the Honored Dharma, and all the worthy sages.
Throughout boundless buddha-fields, they perform the buddha-work. (At this point, cease chanting. Scatter flowers as an offering. Holding an incense burner in hand, form this mental visualization:)
The essence of all the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha Jewels is eternally pervasive and omnipresent, existing nowhere not.
I pray that by means of these incense and flowers, they may become equal to the *dharmatā*, universally perfuming all Buddha-fields and performing the work of a Buddha.
May all the requisites for offering in the ten directions exist at all times. Now, with all the various kinds of offerings existing throughout the ten directions...
Various kinds of fragrant flowers, necklaces, banners, flags, precious canopies, and all manner of exquisite ornaments; various kinds of music, lamps, candles, food and drink,
clothing, bedding, and medicinal decoctions— even including every kind of ornamental article for making offerings throughout the entirety of the ten directions—
one should, through recollection and mental visualization, offer these universally together with all sentient beings as a tribute of worship.
I rejoice in all those throughout every world who are currently practicing offerings.
As for those who have not yet practiced offerings, may they be inspired and guided to do so.
Furthermore, may my own body swiftly reach every buddha-field, and at each site of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, perform every kind of adorned offering.

Together with all sentient beings, I equally offer these articles to make offerings to the Dharma-body, the Form-body, the relics, the images, and the stupas and temples of all Buddhas; to all Buddhist activities;
to all treasuries of the Dharma and all places where the Dharma is preached; and to the entire assembly of noble and holy Sangha. May [this merit] be shared with all...
After sentient beings have performed such offerings and practiced them in this way, they gradually achieve the six pāramitās and the four immeasurable minds.
They come to deeply understand that all phenomena are fundamentally quiescent, neither arising nor ceasing, and are of a single flavor and equality.
Free from conceptual thought and pure; ultimately perfect. (This section uses the scriptural text in its entirety. Having formed this thought, chant:
Having made offerings, with all reverence. (One prostration.)
(Section Four: Invocation of the Triple Gem and the Celestial Beings) [This scripture contains no formal method for invocation.

According to other ritual protocols, it is appropriate to perform three invocations on the first day of the rite. This is because, although the Triple Gem is omnipresent, sentient beings have long accumulated delusion, turning their backs on awakening and uniting with the dust of sensory objects; thus, mindfulness and compassion have been separated.

Now that they have overturned their confusion and returned to enlightenment, they must contemplate the Triple Gem, which fills all of space and manifests forms according to conditions, like the moon reflected in water. Having formed this thought, with tears and earnest devotion, one should perform the three invocations for each station while holding [the ritual implements] in hand.]
Incense burner. Burn various famous incenses and chant these words with a single mind:
"Homage to our Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha. (Visualize thus: "The nature of my three karmas is like empty space; Śākyamuni Tathāgata is likewise.

Arising from the limit of reality for the sake of sentient beings, he comes together with the assembly to receive this offering. Hereafter, all [invocations] follow this pattern, merely changing the name of the Buddha, his physical appearance, and the place from which he comes. When reaching the invitation of the worthy sages, say: "All worthy sages..."
Thus it is. All other cases should be understood accordingly. Having completed the three requests, perform one prostration.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat the Seven Buddhas of the Past, beginning with Vipaśyin;
with single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat the Fifty-three Buddhas, beginning with Samantaprabhāsa.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat all the physical bodies (*rūpakāya*), *śarīra* relics, images, stūpas, temples, and all Buddha-works of all Buddhas.

(Visualize thus: "The Dharma-body of all Buddhas is like space; its manifested activities abide in the world beyond conception. I now entreat with my three karmas according to the Dharma; I pray that you will manifest your presence and accept this offering.")
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time.

With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat the subtle and wondrous Dharma-treasury of the *Sūtra on Examining Good and Evil Karmic Retribution*. (Recite this visualization: The nature of phenomena is like space, invisible;
The eternally abiding Dharma-jewel is inconceivable. I now entreat you with my three karmas according to the Dharma; May you manifest your presence and accept these offerings.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat the Dharma-treasuries of all the ten directions (visualize as above).
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat all the worthy ones and sages of the ten directions.

With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sthira-viśuddha-śraddhā (this is the person who, being responsive to the occasion, initiates the teaching; one should keep this bodhisattva in mind).
For our sake, you have inquired about the Great Dharma. That we are now able to hear this most supreme teaching is entirely due to the immense kindness and virtue of the Bodhisattvas.
With single-minded devotion, we take refuge in and entreat Namah Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

One should contemplate the compassionate and wise conduct of these two Bodhisattvas, who universally deliver all deluded beings; their majestic spiritual power is no different from that of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.
With single-minded devotion, we take refuge in and entreat Namah Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. (One should reflect: "This one is our master for the confession of transgressions.

By virtue of this Bodhisattva’s great compassion and majestic spiritual power, may there be no evil that is not extinguished, and no goodness that does not arise. I now take refuge and offer my petition like a child remembering its mother; he is the primary presiding lord of this place of practice. As for all other Buddhas and Bodhisattvas..."

Together, bear witness to this. With tears and wailing, we seek your compassion as if we were personally before you. We earnestly hope that the Bodhisattva will graciously accept us and protect us. One should contemplate the verses as described above.

With single-minded devotion, we invoke the Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of spirits, and all the holy assemblies who protect the True Dharma within the monastery (in each case, perform three invocations; however, prostrations may be omitted; there is no hindrance for laypeople).
I only pray that Śākyamuni, the Compassionate Father; the Seven Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; the Fifty-three Buddhas; all the Awakened Ones;

those with the eye of the path of others' minds; those with unimpeded vision and hearing; and those with mastery over the supernormal powers of the body, will descend upon this site of practice to gather us in and cause us to achieve pure faith.
[This concerns] the Honored Scripture on the Divination of the Retribution of Good and Evil Karma, the Pure Dharma-Treasury of the Ten Directions, and so forth.
The true *dharmatā* fills all of space; may it manifest at this site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to accept my offerings.

May the Bodhisattva Firm Pure Faith, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and all the worthies and sages of the ten directions, without abandoning their great compassion, descend upon this Dharma seat.
Out of pity, may they protect and shelter me, and bear witness to my practice of the Dharma. Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva...

Sā. O Savior, True Person, Greatly Wise Bodhisattva, Skillful Speaker of Consolation, Swift Remover of All Obstacles and Increaser of Pure Faith, Possessor of Great Loving-Kindness and Great Compassion, who does not violate your original vow: emit great radiance and fulfill my aspirations.
O Dharma-protecting devas, nāgas, kinnaras, and true lords, come at my invocation; steadfastly guard this site of enlightenment and repel all demonic obstacles. Reveal...

Manifest auspiciousness! May that which I cultivate achieve sovereign accomplishment. (Recite this three times at each section while holding the incense burner, then perform one prostration—except where there is a protector of the Dharma, in which case prostration is not required;
for laypeople, it is not an impediment).

(Fifth: Praise and Homage to the Triple Gem) [The sutra contains no formal praise of the Dharma, nor is there a separate section established for it. However, taking two verses from the *Daśacakra-kṣitigarbha-bodhisattva-sūtra* in which Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva praises the Buddha, and performing prostrations in accordance with them, these are combined into a single section.]
I have heard that you are an ocean of universal knowledge, With boundless and true virtues;
Delivering all sentient beings, I rejoice and pay homage. Having cultivated immeasurable merit in the past, You now attain the worship of your venerable feet;
May I, throughout immeasurable eons, Constantly practice manifold offerings.

With single-minded reverence, I pay homage to the past Buddha Vipaśyin. (Contemplate thus: "The nature of both the one who pays homage and the object of homage is empty and quiescent; the resonance between cause and response is inconceivable.

My place of practice is like a jewel of Indra, within which the image of Vipaśyin Buddha appears. My own body and shadow appear before the Tathāgata; with head meeting his feet, I take refuge and pay homage. To seek the cessation of obstacles, one should prostrate at the feet [of the Buddha]. Alternatively, one may also address the request according to whatever one seeks; for example, if seeking the *vinaya* vows, one says: "I prostrate at your feet to seek the *vinaya* vows. This applies similarly to seeking the realization of the fruits [of the path], seeking rebirth [in a pure land], and so forth.

(Sixth: The Practice of Repentance) The Sūtra states: "One should confess the transgressions committed and address [the Buddha] with single-minded devotion. Although transgressions are immeasurable, those manifested through the wheel of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) are particularly grave. They can summon evil retributions and obstruct the Noble Path; therefore, one must feel shame and remorse.

With tears streaming down their faces, each recounted his own transgressions and earnestly repented, hoping for their total eradication. Prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, they finished speaking of their grave offenses and then formed this thought:
I and all sentient beings have, since beginningless time, been constantly obstructed by the heavy offenses of the three karmas and six sense faculties.
We have failed to see the Buddhas and have not known the essential way of escape; we have merely followed the cycle of birth and death, remaining ignorant of the wondrous principle.
Although I now know it, I still share with all sentient beings the obstruction of every heavy offense. Now, before Kṣitigarbha and the Buddhas of the ten directions, universally...

For the sake of all sentient beings, I take refuge and repent. I pray only that you will grant your protection and cause all obstacles to be extinguished. (Having formed this thought, kneel on the right knee and proclaim:)
For the sake of all sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm, I vow to sever and eliminate the three obstructions; I take refuge and repent.
(Having chanted this, prostrate with the five limbs touching the ground, and further reflect thus:)
From beginningless time until now, I and all sentient beings, due to craving and false views, have: (1) internally clung to the notions of self and person;
(2) externally associated with evil friends; (3) failed to rejoice in even a hair’s breadth of another’s merit; (4) extensively committed various transgressions through the three karmic doors;
(5) and although the specific acts were not numerous, the evil intent was pervasive, continuing day and night without interruption.
(6) Concealing and hiding one’s faults, not wishing for others to know them; (7) not fearing the evil realms; (8) lacking a sense of shame and a lack of dread of blame;
(9) denying the existence of cause and effect. Therefore, on this day, (1) one should have deep faith in cause and effect;
(2) give rise to profound shame and dread of blame; (3) give rise to great fear; (4) openly confess and repent; (5) sever the mind of continuity; and (6) resolve upon Bodhicitta.

6. With the mind, sever evil and cultivate good. 7. Diligently restrain the three karmas to overturn the heavy transgressions of the past. 8. Rejoice in even a hair’s breadth of merit, whether performed by ordinary beings or sages.

9. Mindfully recollect that the Buddhas of the ten directions possess great merit and wisdom, capable of rescuing and delivering myself and all sentient beings from the sea of the two deaths and establishing us on the shore of the three virtues. 10. Since beginningless time, we have not known the true nature of all phenomena.
The fundamental nature is empty and quiescent. Having extensively committed various evils, I now realize this emptiness and quiescence;
for the sake of seeking Bodhi and for the sake of sentient beings, I shall extensively cultivate all manner of goodness and universally sever all evils (10).
I only pray that the Triple Gem and Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva will compassionately accept me and grant me leave to repent. (Having formed this thought, kneel on the right knee and proclaim:)
I, disciple [Name], repent with a sincere heart. I and all sentient beings are pure by nature; we share the same reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) as the essence of all Buddhas.

Yet, due to the causal conditions of the habitual perfuming of the darkness of ignorance and delusion, illusory objects appear, causing us to give rise to thoughts of attachment and to calculate "self" and "what belongs to self.
We practice various unwholesome dharmas, and through the three karmas and six sense faculties, we extensively commit manifold transgressions—the ten evil deeds and the five...

This is contrary [to the Dharma]. To disparage what is grave while treating what is light as an obstacle, and to obstruct wisdom, obstruct meditative concentration, and obstruct all categories of ethical discipline, causes one to sink long into the ocean of suffering with no prospect of escape.

Even if one wishes to practice, there will be many obstacles of doubt; one may be disturbed by external māras or encounter wrong views, resulting in a lack of conducive conditions and the failure to achieve pure faith. Now that you have encountered...
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha has skillfully offered words of consolation, dispersing the clouds of my delusion and purifying my thoughts and mind.

Seeking refuge and repenting for my transgressions, I pray that all the Great Compassionate Honored Ones of the ten directions will bear witness and protect me with mindfulness. As I now repent, I shall not create [such karma] again. May I and all...

May all sentient beings swiftly eliminate the immeasurable kalpas of offenses—the ten evil deeds, the four grave transgressions, the five heinous crimes, the perverse slandering and reviling of the Triple Gem, and the sins of icchantikas. The nature of such offenses is fundamentally empty and quiescent;
they arise merely from false and inverted minds, having no fixed reality that can be apprehended. May all sentient beings swiftly reach the fundamental source of the mind.

May the roots of sin be eternally extinguished. (One may recite this once or thrice; the same applies to the four [vows] below. Having finished the confession, take refuge and pay homage to the Triple Gem.

(This text of confession, along with the three vows below, is all derived from the original sutra. However, prior to the words "I only pray," a few phrases from other parts of the sutra have been excerpted to express the intent of single-mindedly looking up to the Buddhas to report one's committed offenses.
Aside from these, not a single character has been dared to be altered. (The Seventh Vow: The Vow of Exhortation and Entreaty)
I, disciple [Name], with a sincere heart, make this entreaty: may all Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions who have not yet attained perfect enlightenment swiftly attain it;
and those who have already attained perfect enlightenment, may they remain forever in the world, turning the wheel of the sublime Dharma and not entering parinirvāṇa.
Having made this entreaty, I take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem.
(Eighth: Making the Vow of Rejoicing) I, disciple [Name], with a sincere heart rejoice.
May I and all sentient beings ultimately and forever abandon the mind of envy, and may we [rejoice] in all merits cultivated and studied throughout all lands in the three periods of time.
And all those who have attained accomplishment, may they all rejoice. Having rejoiced, I take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem.
(The Ninth Aspiration for Dedication:
I, disciple [Name], with a sincere heart, dedicate [these merits]. May all the merit I have cultivated serve to benefit one...
May all sentient beings alike proceed toward the Buddha-wisdom and reach the city of Nirvana. Having thus dedicated [the merit], take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem.
(Tenth: Supplemental Vow and Sitting Upright in a Quiet Room to Recite the Name)

(Regarding the Dharma-gate of the Five Repentances: there is a separate section for making vows, which is not mentioned in this sutra. This is likely because the three practices of Exhortation and so forth are themselves the essence of vows. Furthermore, practitioners who cultivate this method of repentance have differing goals:

some seek ethical discipline (*śīla*), some seek meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), some seek rebirth in the Pure Land, and some seek peace and happiness in the present life. Now, because the decision is made by lot, it is permitted to supplement these vows; however, this must be personally declared by each practitioner and cannot be predetermined in fixed words.

Nevertheless, although the specific vows sought differ, they must accord with the Four Great Vows and must not increase the cycle of birth and death. Fearing that one might be unaware of the general outline and thus contravene the core intent of the sutra, I shall briefly set forth the essential meaning to facilitate practice. Whether to employ this or not is left to the individual.)
[Leave it to their own discernment].
I, disciple [Name], with a sincere heart make this vow:
May the Triple Gem of the ten directions, and the Compassionate Honored One Kṣitigarbha, take pity upon me, protect and sustain me, and deliver and rescue me, so that this land—

Calamities and disturbances shall be eliminated; the True Dharma shall circulate; all shall give rise to pure faith; there shall be no obstacles; and the demonic and heterodox shall be forever severed.

My own and those of all sentient beings’ heavy karmic offenses shall be swiftly extinguished; we shall be free from decline and affliction in this present life; our livelihoods shall be fully provided for; and the roots of the three clusters of precepts shall be established.

Ultimately pure, the two paths of contemplation should manifest before one’s mind. One will fully accomplish samādhi, dhāraṇī, supernatural powers, skillful means, the four methods of attraction, and the six perfections.
Having realized the single reality realm of one's own mind, one shall leave this body for the next world.
Born before the Buddha, they personally attend Amitābha;

having served successive Buddhas, they receive direct predictions of enlightenment. Returning to the midst of worldly toil, they universally gather the deluded masses to together enter the secret treasury.
Having made this vow, they take refuge and pay homage to the Triple Gem.
Taking refuge in the Buddha, may all sentient beings realize the Great Way and give rise to the unsurpassed mind.
Taking refuge in the Dharma, may all sentient beings enter deeply into the treasury of the scriptures, with wisdom as vast as the ocean.
Taking refuge in the Sangha, may all sentient beings lead and manage great assemblies, free from all hindrances.

I pay homage to the assembly of noble ones. (Next, proceed to another quiet chamber. Sit upright with a single mind. Whether reciting aloud or silently contemplating, [invoke] Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva. For those whose mental obscurations are many, they should circumambulate within the ritual site while reciting and contemplating, three times during the day and three times at night, exactly as described in the sūtra.
After seven days, every morning, one should frequently cast the second wheel three times. If one’s body, speech, and mind are entirely pure and virtuous, this is called attaining purity.

If one does not obtain the signs of the wheel indicating the purity of the three karmas, then even if one sees radiant light, extraordinary fragrances, auspicious dreams, and the like, these are merely false appearances and are not virtuous signs. Until the signs of the wheel indicating the purity of the three karmas are obtained, one is permitted only to recite the name of Kṣitigarbha.)

It is not permitted to practice the methods of contemplation until one has attained the auspicious signs (*śubhanimitta*); only thereafter may one practice them according to reality within the two types of contemplative paths. Section Six: A Separate Explanation of the Two Types of Contemplative Paths.

(The single section on "Repentance and Seated Meditation" is practiced at the time of exiting the altar after the repentance is finished; therefore, it is listed as the tenth among the formal practices.

These two contemplations of the present sutra require that one first undergo the purity of repentance before being permitted to practice them formally; therefore, they are explained separately only after the ten sections have concluded.)

The Sūtra says: "When those sentient beings have merely learned to cultivate a sincere mind and have caused their body, speech, and mind to attain the mark of purity, I shall likewise protect and keep them in mind, until they are capable of practicing the various dhyānas and wisdoms. It further says:
"If there are sentient beings who wish to enter the Mahāyāna, they should first know the fundamental karma of their initial practice."
This means that one relies upon a single, ultimate reality as the objective sphere to cultivate faith and understanding. Furthermore, it says:

"If one wishes to rely upon a single, ultimate reality to cultivate faith and understanding, one should train in two types of contemplative paths: first, the contemplation of mind-only consciousness."

Second is the true contemplation of suchness. One who trains in the contemplation of consciousness-only should, at all times and in all places, observe whatever actions are performed by body, speech, or mind, knowing them all to be nothing but mind.

Even regarding all objective spheres, if the mind dwells upon them, one should examine and know them all, ensuring that the mind does not engage in indeterminate攀緣 (pān-luán-yuán / *ālambana*). Do not...
One should self-awaken and, in every moment of thought, examine everything accordingly.

Whenever the mind has an object of focus or a recollection, one should cause the mind to follow that recollection and make the mind self-aware. One should know that these thoughts and conceptualizations arise spontaneously within one's own inner mind;
it is not the case that all objective realms possess thought or discrimination. In this way, one should maintain mindfulness and awareness of the inner mind. Thus should one know.

There are only deluded thoughts; there are no real objects. Do not allow this practice to cease or be abandoned. This is called the cultivation and study of the contemplation of mind-only consciousness.
Moment by moment, one contemplates and knows that it is only the mind that arises and perishes, like flowing water or the flame of a lamp, never remaining still for even a moment.
From this, one shall attain the Samādhi of the Tranquility of Form. Having attained this samādhi, one should next train in and learn śamatha with faith.

Regarding the contemplation of the mind: those who practice the contemplation of the mind through faith in *vipaśyanā* and study the true contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness) contemplate that the nature of the mind is neither arising nor ceasing, does not abide in seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, and is free from all conceptual discriminations.

Gradually, they are able to transcend the objective marks of the four formless concentrations (*ārūpyasamādhi*) and attain a semblance of the *śūnyatā-samādhi* (emptiness samādhi), whereby they can successively enter the mind.

In the samādhi of tranquility, one is further able to enter the *ekavyūha-samādhi* (one-practice samādhi), where one beholds countless Buddhas and gives rise to a profound and expansive mind, abiding in the stage of firm faith (*adhimukti*).
This refers to attaining decisive faith and understanding in the two paths of contemplation—*śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*—and being decisively oriented toward them.
Furthermore, regarding those who practice and study with the aforementioned faith and understanding, there are two types of persons.

There are two types. The first consists of those with sharp faculties who have already been able to know that all external objects are merely produced by the mind, being deceptive and unreal like dreams or illusions, possessing certainty without doubt, having light and subtle hindrances and obscurations, and little mental distraction.

Such persons as these should immediately study the true contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness). Second, there are those of dull faculties who have not yet been able to know that all external objects are merely mind;
their emotional attachments are deep-seated, hindrances arise frequently, and their minds are difficult to subdue.
They should first study the contemplation of consciousness-only (*cittamātra*). Now, based on the scriptural text, I shall briefly set forth its meaning. This...
The essence of this sutra is the single reality realm (*eka-tattva-dhātu*). Its primary tenet is the two-fold path of contemplation.
Without a profound and clear illumination of the single reality realm, one cannot give rise to the two contemplations in accordance with the nature of reality.

Without the diligent cultivation of these two contemplations, one cannot realize and harmonize with the single reality realm. This single reality realm is none other than the inconceivable (*acintya*).

The "object" (*viṣaya*) is also called the "true reality of all phenomena" (*dharmatā*). This means that the object is the phenomena themselves; the single reality is the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

The object is the three thousandfold world as actualized through events (*ji*), while the single reality is the three thousandfold world as inherent in principle (*li*). The object is the provisional (*upāya*), and the single reality is the ultimate (*paramārtha*).
Since the provisional and the ultimate are non-dual, and principle and phenomena are of one suchness, it is called the "object of the single reality. Furthermore, by means of the object...
When the realm proceeds from the one reality, then the one is empty and all are empty; this is the inconceivable ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
When the one reality proceeds from the objective sphere, then the one is provisional and all are provisional; this is the inconceivable conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

To speak directly of the objective sphere of the one reality, then the one is the center and all are the center; this is the inconceivable Middle Way, the supreme truth of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-satya*). Therefore—
The Sūtra says: "The deluded mind ultimately has no substance, for it cannot be seen.
If there were no cognizant faculty capable of discrimination, then there would be no differentiated characteristics of all realms throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Is this not precisely the meaning of emptiness? It further says: "That which is without the characteristic of discrimination is omnipresent in all places, because it is able..."
Because it serves as the support and basis for the establishment of all phenomena, is this not precisely the meaning of "provisional" (prajñapti)?
Furthermore, it says: "The essence of the sentient beings' mind is, from the very beginning, neither arising nor ceasing; its self-nature is pure. It also says:
"One should know that all phenomena are collectively termed 'mind,' because their essential nature is not different [from the mind] and they are subsumed within the mind. It further says: "One..."
The various retributions of all sentient beings are all established and grown in dependence upon the Dharma-body of the Buddhas.
Abiding within the Dharma-body, they are encompassed by the sphere of the Dharma-body; taking the Dharma-body as their essence, there is nothing that can transcend the boundaries of the Dharma-body.
Is this not precisely the meaning of the "Middle"? Thus, one knows that the realm of the single reality is already [present].

This fully encapsulates the purport of a single verse from the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*. "Phenomena" (*viṣaya*) refers to those dharmas produced by causes and conditions; "the one reality" (*eka-tattva*) is precisely emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* focuses on contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), and thus first establishes the objective realm (*viṣaya*). This sutra reveals the truths (*satya*), and thus first sets forth the principle (*tattva*).

By relying upon this single reality as the objective realm to cultivate faith and understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*), one comes to know that the two paths of contemplation are entirely [contained therein].
This is an inconceivable Dharma-gate. Furthermore, regarding the differentiation within it of those who are sharp and those who are dull, two general meanings may be briefly set forth.
First: although this sutra correctly elucidates the fundamental tenet of the Perfect and Sudden (yuan-dun), it also encompasses those of the Separate (bie) capacity;

thus, the Perfect is termed "sharp" and the Separate is termed "dull. Second: even among those of the Perfect capacity, there is still a further differentiation between the sharp and the dull. This refers to the first meaning.
This refers to the practitioner of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Within the stage of names (*mingziwei*), they are able to know the secret treasury of the Tathāgata;

thus, their physical eye is itself called the Buddha-eye. Consequently, they are able to train in the true contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness) and fully comprehend the nature of mind present before them.
Originally unborn, it does not undergo further extinction; this is what is called the single characteristic of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Although the three thousand worlds appear vividly distinct, they are ultimately equal. This is precisely the method for first practicing contemplation within the stage of names and words.

One attains the semblance Samādhi of Emptiness, ascends to the fifth grade, and perfectly subdues the five abodes of ignorance; thus, one transcends the meditative concentrations of emptiness and so forth.

Regarding the signs of the meditative object (*ālambana-nimitta*): upon entering the samādhi of mental tranquility, one is immediately able to enter the *ekavyūha-samādhi* (one-practice samādhi) and abide in the stage of firm faith (*adhimukti*).
This is what is called the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-pariśuddhi*), which is the semblance of Buddhahood.

Therefore, regarding the two paths of contemplation—*śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*—one attains decisive faith and understanding and is able to decisively advance toward them; for *śamatha* is... [not]... [the ultimate].
The three types of *śamatha* are inconceivable; *vipaśyanā* is the three types of inconceivable *vipaśyanā*.

The non-duality of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is precisely the *prajñā* of the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) and the ultimate liberation of *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*. This is partially realized at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), where it manifests spontaneously.
Within the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), this is called "attaining certainty. As for practitioners of the Separate Teaching (*pṛthag-deśanā*), [this occurs] at the level of names...
While within this stage, although one hears of the Middle Way, one is not yet able to fully comprehend it and can only believe in it with reverence;

therefore, one must first study the contemplation of mind-only consciousness to realize that external objects do not truly exist and that there is only the internal mind—this is precisely the entry from the conventional into emptiness.

It is not that there is no sequential order; therefore, one first attains the samādhi of the tranquility of form (*rūpa-śānti*). By analogy with the stages, this should correspond to the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) in the Distinct Teaching (*byed-pa'i chos*).
If viewed from the perspective of the Perfect Teaching (*yongs-rdzogs kyi chos*), its stage corresponds to the five ranks (*lnga-sku*).

Next, one should study and practice the two contemplations of śamatha and vipaśyanā based on faith; this constitutes the instruction to abandon the Distinct and follow the Perfect. The subsequent intent concerns those of sharp faculties in the Perfect Teaching.
Within the essence of the conscious mind, its fundamental nature is quiescent; the three thousand [realms] are, in their full manifestation, precisely emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

Therefore, it is said that one should immediately practice the true contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness). For those who are somewhat dull-witted, they must first illuminate the arising of the mind and observe how the transformation and construction of the ten realms are precisely emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.
Therefore, it is said that they should first study the contemplation of consciousness-only (*cittamātra-vijñaptimātra*). However, regarding this one...

The realm of reality (*bhūtadhātu*). If one is well able to grasp its meaning, then it arises in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*). Although the functions of these two contemplations differ, in reality there is no superiority or inferiority between them.

Regarding the difference in their functions, as stated in the *Xiangjie* (Detailed Explanation): "The contemplation of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) proceeds through phenomena (*vastu*), while the contemplation of True Suchness (*tathatā*) contemplates principle (*li*).

Contemplating the originally quiescent three thousand [worlds] as principle is called the contemplation of principle; illuminating the mind's arising transformations that construct the ten realms is called the contemplation of phenomena."

Regarding contemplation (*guan*): from the perspective of principle (*li*), one penetrates the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); from the perspective of phenomena (*shi*), one focuses exclusively on illuminating the arising of the mind.

Furthermore, directly contemplating that a single thought-moment inherently possesses the three thousand realms is called "contemplation of principle" (*li-guan*). Allowing the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) to function freely throughout the four modes of mental activity (*catur-yoga*) and investigating the arising mind as it transforms and constructs the ten realms is called "contemplation of phenomena" (*shi-guan*).
Therefore, the ancients categorized these based on whether the mind arises or does not arise, and whether one investigates the movement [of the mind] or does not investigate it.

Regarding the division of fortune and the statement that there is no superiority or inferiority: as explained in detail, one must understand that the knowledge gained through divination is solely mind.

Thus, one does not give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) or external objects. Therefore, the Sūtra speaks of the "Samādhi of the Quiescence of Form" (*rūpa-śānti-samādhi*);
this does not mean that the contemplation of phenomena focuses exclusively on external forms. Rather, it refers to the true contemplation of *tathatā*, which contemplates the nature of the mind.
Birth is non-extinguishing. Because one can transcend the four formless emptinesses (*ārūpya-śūnyatā*), both mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are utterly quiescent.
Therefore, the Sūtra speaks of the "Samādhi of Quiescent Mind. This does not mean that the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*) resides solely within the internal mind. Furthermore, it says:

"One who cultivates the contemplation of principle, though it is said they contemplate only that which is inherently complete (*li-jù*), must know that the entirety of cultivation (*xiū*) resides in the nature (*xìng*). Thus, one truly cultivates reality.

This is the contemplation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). One who practices the contemplation of phenomena (*dharma*) must understand that although they contemplate the mind capable of creating the ten realms, the entirety of nature (*prakṛti*) constitutes cultivation;
thus, they are correctly practicing the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*). Furthermore, the *Yiyao chao* states:

"One should know that when contemplating the internal mind, both contemplations are thus; when contemplating external objects, both contemplations are likewise so. Based on this, [it follows that] one...

A single form, a single fragrance, a single particle, and a single dharma—all are understood to be mind-only; they all return to the same reality. Expedient means applied according to what is appropriate are ultimately no different.

Furthermore, although these two contemplations are said to be practiced only after one has attained the signs of purity through repentance, they are nonetheless present when performing the actual practice of repentance and reciting the name of Kṣitigarbha. It is as when practicing...

At the time of repentance, beginning from the offerings of incense and flowers and ending with the three refuges, one proceeds through these matters with clarity, directing the mind without obstruction, knowing that they are produced solely by the mind and that there are no real objective realms; this is called the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
If, from the initial offerings up to the three refuges, although the activities are distinct, the single mind does not arise, this is called the contemplation of true suchness (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, when reciting the name, one clearly perceives each syllable with distinct clarity and realizes that the mind is like an illusion.
The great name of Kṣitigarbha is not separate from one's own mind; this is called the "contemplation of mind-only consciousness.

If one contemplates the Dharma-body of Kṣitigarbha and the Dharma-bodies of all Buddhas as being equal in essence to one's own body—without duality or distinction, unborn and undying, and eternally blissful—[this is the contemplation of the equality of the three bodies].
The self is pure; its merits are perfected. This is called the true contemplation of suchness (*tathatā*).

Furthermore, once these auspicious signs have been attained, when one is correctly practicing the two contemplations, one may still continue to practice the methods of repentance and recite the Name as before.

By means of these repentances and the recitation of the Name, the two contemplations are assisted and brought to even greater clarity. This is why the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate of the Five Repentances exists.
From the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) up to the level of Equal Enlightenment (*samabodhi*), there is nothing that does not employ this as a skillful means for cultivation.

One must understand that the three types of repentance—repentance through ritual action (*vidhi-karma*), repentance by grasping signs (*nimitta-grahaṇa*), and repentance of non-arising (*anutpāda*)—are such that each subsequent one contains the preceding, while each preceding one also permeates the subsequent.
When phenomena and principle support one another, remaining consistent from beginning to end, it alone may be called a Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*) Dharma-gate. Should one treat it lightly...
Suddenly encountering worldly affairs, one may engage in lofty discourse on names and principles; yet heavy karmic offenses will not be extinguished, and wholesome dharmas will not arise.

Therefore, practitioners in the final age must urgently seek to realize the earnest intent with which the Bodhisattva Jianjingxin questioned the Dharma, and must deeply investigate the original purpose behind the establishment of the Dharma by the Great Being Kṣitigarbha.
One should do so with a heart of truth that is free from deception, a heart that is never negligent, and with a sense of profound urgency.
Regarding the mind of birth and death and the unsurpassed Great Bodhicitta, within this sutra one develops correct understanding and accomplishes true cultivation.
One attains firm faith and does not fall into the obstacle of doubt; were it otherwise, it would be like encountering a meal and yet refusing to eat.
The precious mountain is returned empty-handed; even the True Being who saves the world and the Greatly Wise Bodhisattva can do nothing about it. Appendix:
The Method for Divining the Wheel Signs.
With a sincere heart, pay reverent homage to all Buddhas of the ten directions.
May all sentient beings of the ten directions swiftly attain the opportunity to draw near to, make offerings to, and freely receive the true Dharma.
With a sincere heart, I pay homage to all the treasuries of the Dharma throughout the ten directions.
May all sentient beings throughout the ten directions swiftly attain the ability to receive, uphold, read, and recite [this teaching],
practice it according to the Dharma, and explain it to others.
With a sincere heart, I pay homage to all the worthy and holy ones throughout the ten directions.
May all sentient beings throughout the ten directions swiftly attain the opportunity to draw near to and make offerings to [the Buddha], resolve their minds upon Bodhi,
and reach the stage of non-retrogression.
With a sincere heart, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha.
May all sentient beings throughout the ten directions swiftly eliminate their heavy karmic offenses and evil deeds, be free from all obstacles, and have every necessity for life fully provided.
(Having thus prostrated, one should offer whatever incense, flowers, and other items are available, making this proclamation:)
Respectfully holding incense and flowers, make offerings according to the Dharma.
May these clouds of incense and flowers pervade the realms of the ten directions, making offerings to all Buddhas, the Honored Dharma, and all the worthy sages.
Throughout boundless Buddha-lands, they perform the work of Buddhas. (At this point, cease chanting; scatter flowers as an offering, and again cultivate the visualization, saying:
"All the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha... (and so forth) ...free from conceptual thought, pure, and ultimately perfect. (The full text is contained within the *Chanyi*.)

One must become thoroughly proficient in this so that the mental visualization proceeds without obstruction. Having completed the offerings, one should pay all due respect (performing one prostration). Next, using separate incense and flowers, one should focus the mind on making offerings to Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva and address him with single-minded devotion:

"I, disciple [Name], am currently an ordinary person subject to birth and death. My karmic obstructions are profound and heavy; I do not understand the causes and conditions of the retributions of the three periods of time and harbor many doubts. Now, regarding this matter, I respectfully rely upon the three types of wheel-signs shown by the Bodhisattva to perform divination according to the Dharma.

With a sincere heart, I look up and appeal to the Compassionate Honored One, Kṣitigarbha. I pray that you will empower me with the power of your great compassion to rescue and sustain me, and remove my obstructive doubts. Having spoken these words, one should prostrate oneself fully, casting the five limbs upon the ground.
Kneel with the right knee on the ground and join the palms. With single-minded devotion, recite:
"Namo Dizang Pusa Mahasattva" (either calling the name aloud or reciting it silently). Continue until you have completed one thousand recitations, at which point make this formal declaration:

"O Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, endowed with great kindness and great compassion, I pray that you will protect and mind me and all sentient beings, swiftly removing all obstacles and increasing pure faith, so that what I now observe may correspond to reality.

(Having spoken these words, hold the wheel-mark with both hands, support it with a clean object, and with utmost sincerity and gravity, toss it upward with palms facing up. Observe and examine it closely; thus one shall know whether it corresponds or does not correspond, just as explained in the sutra. One must first thoroughly study the text of the sutra oneself to understand this.)

The general meaning is as follows: Only then may one cast the wheels; otherwise, one will naturally lack a refined mind and, conversely, suspect the wheels to be a futile arrangement, thereby incurring great sin.

(Whenever one divines the signs of the wheels—whether intending to divine all three types of wheel-signs—one should perform prostrations, make offerings, recite the names [of the Buddhas], and make a formal declaration (*kṣānti*). Only then should one divine the signs of the first wheel. One must attend closely to every single good or evil sign manifested within the first wheel and separately divine the signs of the second wheel.

Next, one should again divine the signs of the third wheel. If there is a desire to practice the methods of repentance (*pūjā-vidhi*) and one divines only the first and second wheels, one should likewise perform prostrations and offerings.)

Recite the name [of the deity], perform the ritual announcement (*śveta*), and examine the signs in sequence. If one acts for oneself or for others, one should examine only the signs of the third wheel. Those who wish to know matters concerning the karmic retribution of the three periods of time should likewise perform prostrations, offerings, recite the name, and make the ritual announcement;

they should take the signs of the third wheel and cast it three times in succession, recording the number of appearances to discern good or ill fortune. If one has practiced repentance for seven days and wishes to examine only the signs of the second wheel to seek purely auspicious omens, one need only perform the ritual announcement at dawn and cast it three times in succession.

Homage to the fifty-three Buddhas. Homage to all Buddhas of the ten directions.
